newsitem.title: INDIA: Survivors describe "hell" in India cinema inferno.
newsitem.headline: Survivors describe "hell" in India cinema inferno.

text.p: Survivors described hellish scenes in an Indian cinema blaze on Friday that killed 58 people, with film-goers stampeding in panic and women with children in their arms leaping from windows.
Most of the victims, trapped on smoke-filled upper floors, died of suffocation, firemen and doctors said.

"Once the fire broke...it was like hell, people were running like mad...jumping over each other, everyone wanted to rush out of the exit doors," said 34-year-old shopkeeper Uday Pawar, one survivor of the fire that struck on Friday the 13th.
He and his wife Rekha escaped the inferno by jumping out of a window onto the roof of an adjacent building.
"I want to thank the God for saving us, it's a miracle that both of us are still alive. I know some people have lost their whole families," Pawar told Reuters.
Witnesses described scenes of horror.
"I saw women with children in their arms breaking windows and jumping out. It was unbelievable," said one.
About 1,000 people were packed into the New Delhi cinema as the blaze ripped through the 1,050-seat building. Apart from those killed, more than 100 were injured.
An electrical transformer set fire to dozens of cars parked in the cinema's basement. The fire soon leapt to the upper floors and engulfed the entire cinema hall, witnesses said.
Local residents rushed to the scene and helped rescuers to evacuate trapped people, police said.

"The residents in the nearby houses and shops were extremely helpful. They braved the fire, brought in the ropes and saved lots of people before the fire tenders arrived," said a bleeding Devender Chopra.
Chopra injured his hands while trying to break open a window to jump out.
Survivors said most of the people rushed to the bathrooms of the cinema hall. After the blaze, the hall was littered with glass, its walls blackened. Fire authorities feared the roof might cave in.
Most of the dead were thought to have been sitting upstairs in the box and balcony sections, one fireman said. Most of those in the stalls were able to escape.
"As the smoke streamed into the hall people could not see and found it difficult to breathe," said Ajay Bhalla, 27, a local businessman who went to watch the film.
Doctors at the two hospitals where most of the injured were admitted said most of the victims died of suffocation.
"Most of people died due to suffocation and not burns," said S.P. Bajaj, additional medical superintendent at Safdarjung Hospital.
There were heart-rending hospital scenes as relatives identified victims. Several old women were crying as they searched through bodies lying on the floor.
Weeping relatives were desperately going through a list naming the dead stuck outside the entrance of Safdarjung Hospital.
Indira, a seven year old girl, looked with dazed eyes at her mother who lay on the floor at a corner of the casualty ward of the Safdarjung Hospital.
Indira's mother was declared dead by the doctors.
Viewers had thronged the Uphar Grand Cinema in south Delhi for the first show of a popular Hindi film, "Border", which dramatises a 1971 battle between India and Pakistan.
